passages.t: Hand it on; soldier, athlete and farmer
passages.happening:
“You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (verses 1-2).

Then three pictures. “Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him. Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules. The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops” (verses 3-6).

“Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘Be strong’ sounds like a command to try harder. But Paul says where the strength comes from: ‘in the grace that is in Christ Jesus’. Timothy is to be strong the way a branch is strong, by staying joined to what feeds it.

Verse 2 is one of the most important verses about how the faith lasts. Count the people in it. Paul taught Timothy. Timothy is to teach faithful people. They will teach others. That is four generations in one sentence. The gospel is not invented again in each age. It is received and handed on, from one life to the next. The word ‘faithful’ matters here: Paul looks for people who can be trusted, not only people who are clever.

Then come three pictures from everyday life. A Roman soldier served for many years and was expected to give his commander undivided loyalty, keeping clear of ordinary business. An athlete in the Greek games won a wreath, but only if he kept the rules; a cheat lost the prize. A farmer worked hard through the seasons and was the first to eat from the harvest.

Each picture says something different. The soldier: be loyal, and do not let lesser things tangle you up. The athlete: run the right way, not just fast. The farmer: keep working, even when nothing seems to grow, because a harvest comes.

Paul does not explain the pictures fully. ‘Consider what I am saying.’ He trusts Timothy to think, and he trusts the Lord to give understanding.
passages.ot:
Handing on the faith is how Israel lived. Moses handed his work to Joshua in front of all the people: “Be strong and courageous, for you will go with this people into the land” (Deuteronomy 31:7). Elijah handed his work to Elisha, who asked, “Please, let me inherit a double portion of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9). And the psalmist prays, “Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation” (Psalm 71:18).

Proverbs knows the farmer's reward: “Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit” (Proverbs 27:18). And it is the LORD who gives understanding, as Paul says in verse 7: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6).
passages.asks: Paul asks Timothy to hand on what he has received. Ask who taught you the faith, and who you are teaching it to, in your family, your church, or one friendship. Ask which of the three pictures you need most this week: the soldier's loyalty, the athlete's honesty, or the farmer's patience. And ask where your strength is coming from: your own effort, or the grace that is in Christ Jesus.

passages.t: Remember Jesus Christ; the word of God is not chained
passages.happening:
“Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!” (verses 8-9).

“For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
When the work is hard, Paul tells Timothy to remember one person. ‘Remember Jesus Christ.’ And he gives two facts about him.

‘Raised from the dead.’ Jesus is alive. He went through death and came out the other side. That matters all the more because, as Paul says a few verses later, some teachers in Ephesus were saying that the resurrection had already happened in some spiritual way (verse 18). Paul points to the real rising of Jesus.

‘Descended from David.’ Jesus is the promised King from David's family, the one Israel had waited for. He is both the risen Lord and Israel's true King.

Then Paul speaks of his own chains. The word for ‘criminal’ is the same word Luke uses for the two men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:32-33). Paul is being treated like the worst kind of offender. But he adds at once: ‘the word of God cannot be chained’. Rome could lock up the preacher. It could not lock up the message. Paul had seen this before, when his imprisonment helped the gospel spread (Philippians 1:12-14).

Paul endures it all ‘for the sake of the elect’, the people God has chosen, so that they too may be saved. His suffering is not wasted. It is part of how the good news reaches others.
passages.ot:
God promised David a son whose kingdom would last: “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12), and “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). The psalms sing the same promise: “I will establish your offspring forever and build up your throne for all generations” (Psalm 89:4). And Isaiah saw “a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse”, David's father (Isaiah 11:1).

The hope of rising from the dead is there too: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).

And God's word cannot be held back: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8).
passages.asks: Paul says that when things are hard, remember Jesus Christ, raised and reigning. Ask what you most need to remember about him today. Ask whether there is a place in your life where you feel chained, and whether God's word could still be at work there. And ask who might come to faith through what you are willing to endure.

passages.t: A trustworthy saying: dying, living and reigning with him
passages.happening: “This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself” (verses 11-13).
passages.hearers:
‘This is a trustworthy saying’ is Paul's way of marking words the church already knew and he stands behind. Many readers think this saying was an early hymn or confession, sung or said together. It has four lines, each beginning with ‘if’.

The first two lines are promises. ‘If we died with Him, we will also live with Him.’ Paul teaches elsewhere that believers are joined to Christ in his death and will share his life (Romans 6:8). ‘If we endure, we will also reign with Him.’ Those who keep going through hardship will share his rule.

The third line is a warning. ‘If we deny Him, He will also deny us.’ These are almost the words of Jesus himself: “But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:33).

Then the fourth line surprises. You expect it to say: if we are faithless, he will be faithless too. Instead: ‘He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.’ The pattern breaks. Our faithlessness is met by his faithfulness. He stays true to who he is.

Think of Peter. He denied Jesus three times on the night of his arrest. Yet Jesus came to him after the resurrection and gave him his work again (John 21:15-17). Peter wavered and failed, and he was restored.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament holds the same two notes together. A prophet told King Asa, “The LORD is with you when you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will be found by you, but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you” (2 Chronicles 15:2).

And yet God's faithfulness runs deeper than his people's: “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just. A God of faithfulness without injustice” (Deuteronomy 32:4). “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” (Lamentations 3:22-23). And “God is not a man, that He should lie” (Numbers 23:19).
passages.hard:
‘If we deny Him, He will also deny us’, and then, ‘if we are faithless, He remains faithful’. How do these lines fit together?

Readers hold them together in different ways. Many distinguish denying Christ, a settled and final turning away from him, from being faithless, the wavering and failing that every believer knows. Peter denied Jesus in fear and was restored. On this reading the warning is real, and the promise comforts the weak. Others read the fourth line as a further warning: Christ stays faithful to his own word, including his word of judgment, and so will deny those who deny him. Many prefer the first reading, because elsewhere Paul uses God's faithfulness for his saving care of his people: “The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

Behind this lies a wider question: can a true believer finally fall away? Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those truly saved are kept by God and cannot finally be lost. They read the warning as real and serious, a means God uses to keep his people, and hold that those who finally turn away show they never truly belonged. Much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world holds that a person can turn away and forfeit salvation, and they read the warning more directly. These notes do not choose. The site's note on Romans 8:31-39 sets out both, and so does the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’ Both sides take the warning seriously, and both find hope in Christ's faithfulness.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The saying holds a promise, a warning and a deeper promise. Ask whether you have heard the warning, and whether there is a place where you are quietly turning from Christ. Then ask whether you have heard the last line: when you fail, he stays faithful. And ask whether you treat others who have wavered the way Jesus treated Peter.

passages.t: An approved workman; God's firm foundation
passages.happening:
Paul tells Timothy to warn the believers “to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin” (verse 14).

“Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth” (verse 15).

“But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness, and the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some” (verses 16-18).

“Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity’” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Arguments about words had become a sickness in the church at Ephesus. Paul says they do not build anyone up. They ruin the people listening.

Instead, Timothy is to be a good workman. ‘Approved’ is a word for metal that has been tested and found genuine, or a coin of full weight. And ‘accurately handles’ means, word for word, ‘cuts straight’, as a builder cuts a straight road or a farmer ploughs a straight furrow. Timothy is to follow a straight line with God's word, not wander off into speculation. And his aim is to be approved ‘to God’, not to win the crowd.

Then Paul names two men. Hymenaeus appeared in 1 Timothy 1:20. Philetus is named only here. Their teaching was that ‘the resurrection has already occurred’. They probably meant that believers had already been raised with Christ in some inner, spiritual way, so there was no rising of the body to wait for. Many in the Greek world thought the body was a prison for the soul and found the idea of its rising distasteful. Paul had met the same denial in Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:12). He says it spreads ‘like gangrene’, the rot that eats living flesh.

But the church is not left on shaky ground. ‘God's firm foundation stands.’ A seal marked who owned something. This foundation carries two sayings. The first is God's side: ‘The Lord knows those who are His.’ The second is our side: those who call on him must turn from what is wrong. Both are true at once.
passages.ot:
The first saying on the seal comes from the story of Korah's rebellion against Moses, where Moses says, “Tomorrow morning the LORD will reveal who belongs to Him and who is holy” (Numbers 16:5). Some readers hear the second saying in Moses' words in the same story: “Move away now from the tents of these wicked men” (Numbers 16:26).

The hope of the body's rising, which Hymenaeus denied, is in the prophets: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19), and “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2).

And Proverbs warns against quarrels: “To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14).
passages.hard:
Who were Hymenaeus and Philetus, and why does Paul name them?

We know only what the letters tell us. Hymenaeus appears in 1 Timothy 1:20, where Paul says he had put him out of the church's fellowship, with the hope that he would ‘be taught not to blaspheme’. Here he is still teaching, now with Philetus. Their claim was that the resurrection had already happened, and it was unsettling the faith of some.

Paul names them so that Timothy and the church can recognize the danger. He is not naming them to shame them for sport. He names a teaching that was doing harm, and the people spreading it among the believers. And the hope he gives a few verses later reaches even people like them: that God may grant repentance, and they may come to their senses (verses 25-26).

Why does it matter so much? Because Christians confess that Jesus Christ was bodily raised from the dead, and that his people will be raised too. The resurrection is not only a picture of a new inner life. It is God's promise for the whole person, body and all. Paul says in another letter that if there is no resurrection of the dead, our faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:13-17).
passages.asks: Paul asks Timothy to cut a straight line with God's word. Ask whether you go to the Bible to hear it, or to win arguments. Ask whether there are quarrels over words in your church or your home that are ruining the listeners. And ask what you are hoping for: only a better inner life, or the rising of the body and the world made new.

passages.t: Vessels for honour; the Lord's servant must be kind
passages.happening:
“A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use. So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work” (verses 20-21).

“Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling” (verses 22-23).

“And a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will” (verses 24-26).
passages.hearers:
A wealthy house had dishes and jars of gold and silver for special guests, and pots of wood and clay for everyday jobs, including the dirty ones. Paul turns the picture into a call: be clean, and you will be ready for the Master's best use. The point is not what you are made of. It is whether you are clean and ready.

‘Youthful passions’ may mean more than desires of the body. In a letter full of quarrels, some readers think it includes a young man's love of winning an argument. Paul's answer is to run from those things and run toward righteousness, faith, love and peace, and to do it ‘together’ with others who call on the Lord.

Then comes a portrait of the Lord's servant. Not quarrelsome. Kind to everyone, not only to those who agree. Able to teach. Patient when wronged. And when he must correct someone who opposes him, he does it ‘gently’.

Why gently? Because the goal is not to win. It is that the other person might come back to the truth. And Paul says plainly who can make that happen: ‘God may grant them repentance’. The servant cannot force a change of heart. He can only speak truly and kindly, and pray. Paul even sees the opponents with compassion. They are not simply enemies. They have been caught in a trap, ‘taken captive’, and they need rescue.
passages.ot:
Jeremiah watched a potter at work: “But the vessel that he was shaping from the clay became flawed in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do” (Jeremiah 18:4). Isaiah called those who carried the temple's holy things to be clean: “Touch no unclean thing; come out from it, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD” (Isaiah 52:11).

Proverbs teaches the gentle way: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). It warns that “a quarrelsome man” is like wood for a fire (Proverbs 26:21). And the Servant in Isaiah is gentle with the weak: “A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish” (Isaiah 42:3).

God's heart for those who have gone wrong is the same: “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).
passages.hard:
Does ‘be kind to everyone’ and ‘gently reprove’ mean that a church must be gentle with someone who is doing harm, and keep things quiet?

Paul is speaking about how to correct people who oppose the truth: with patience, not with anger or humiliation. That is a word every church and every leader needs. It rules out bullying, shaming and harsh treatment of people who disagree.

But gentleness never means hiding harm. Kindness to an opponent in an argument is not the same as protecting someone who is hurting others. These verses must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to tell a victim to be ‘gentle’ and stay quiet. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul describes a servant who is kind to everyone and gentle with opponents. Ask how you speak to people who disagree with you, online or in person. Ask whether you want to win, or want them to come home. Ask what you need to run from, and what you need to run toward, and who you could do that with. And ask God for a heart that sees opponents as people caught in a trap, not enemies to defeat.
